_note: Mission Footprints Lab. Each field is labelled: verified (from NASA's own description of the image, linked in `page`), interpretation (our reasoning) or unknown (not stated by NASA, so we do not guess). Descriptions were read through the NASA Image and Video Library API on 15 Nov 2026. The only before/after slider is PIA22223, which NASA describes as two HiRISE images of the same area with closely matched viewing and illumination geometry.

instrument.v: Photographed from inside the Lunar Module. The camera is not named in NASA's description.

shows.v: Two parts of the Early Apollo Scientific Experiments Package: the seismometer far away and the laser reflector closer to the camera. NASA notes the astronauts' footprints are very distinct in the lunar soil.

why.v: A record of where the experiments were set up, taken before the crew left.

learn.v: Where the experiments stood relative to each other and to the lander, and how sharply the fine soil holds a footprint.

cannot.v: Whether the reflector still works today (that comes from laser-ranging records, not photos), or what the footprints look like now.

images.title: Tranquility Base from orbit
images.credit: NASA/GSFC/Arizona State University, PIA12909 "Apollo 11: Second Look"

instrument.v: Not named in NASA's description of this image.

date.v: Published 29 September 2009, one month after LRO's first image of the site. The exact capture date is not given.

shows.v: The Apollo 11 landing site, seen again from orbit to give a new view of the historic site.

why.v: NASA's description says the orbiter passed over the site again, providing a new view.

learn.v: Orbital images let scientists check that hardware left behind is still where it was placed, without landing beside it.

cannot.v: The condition of the materials up close. From orbit, small objects are only a few pixels across.

images.title: Two spacecraft, two and a half years apart

shows.v: Surveyor 3 in the foreground and the Apollo 12 Lunar Module behind it. The LM landed about 600 feet (about 180 m) from Surveyor 3 in the Ocean of Storms.

why.v: The crew documented Surveyor 3 before removing its TV camera and other parts, which were brought back to Earth for scientific examination.

learn.v: Returned parts let scientists examine hardware that had spent about two and a half years on the Moon (April 1967 to November 1969).

cannot.v: Exactly who is pictured. NASA's title names Alan Bean, but the same record's description says Conrad is examining the camera. The record alone cannot settle it, so we do not.

images.title: The first photograph from the surface of Mars

shows.v: Rocks and finely granulated sand or dust about 1.4 m from the camera, with part of footpad #2 at right and dust deposited there at landing.

why.v: It was the lander's first look at its surroundings, minutes after touchdown.

learn.v: NASA's description points out rock shapes, pits and cracks, and apparent signs of wind moving granular material.

cannot.v: NASA itself leaves two questions open. A dark band may come from clouds or dust briefly blocking the Sun. A smooth patch beside a rock may mean the rock was moved during landing, or that fine material piled up there. The photo cannot decide.

instrument.v: Imager for Mars Pathfinder (on the lander)

date.v: During the 1997 surface mission. The exact date is not given in NASA's description.

shows.v: The rover Sojourner as it nears the rock named "Wedge", with part of the "Rock Garden" visible at upper right.

why.v: The lander's camera followed the rover as it drove to rocks the team wanted to study.

learn.v: The rover's position relative to its targets, and the size and shape of nearby rocks.

cannot.v: What the rocks are made of. That needs an instrument touching or measuring the rock, not a picture.

shows.v: Perseverance Valley after the dust storm had substantially cleared. Opportunity appears as a blip.

why.v: To look for the silent rover once the storm cleared.

learn.v: The rover was still where it had stopped, and the storm over the valley had largely cleared.

cannot.v: Whether Opportunity was working, or how much dust covered its solar panels. At this distance the rover is only a blip.

images.title: Phoenix landing site, nearly a decade apart

compare.basis: NASA says both images cover the same area, roughly 300 m wide, and are closely matched in viewing and illumination geometry.

date.v: 20 July 2008 and 21 December 2017, about five Martian years apart, both in northern summer

shows.v: The lander (top), the dark spot where the heat shield hit (right), and the back shell and parachute (bottom) at 68° N.

why.v: To compare how the landing site changed over time.

learn.v: NASA describes the changes: the lander is darker and covered in dust, the heat-shield spot is brighter because of dust, and the parachute has shifted east in the wind.

cannot.v: How thick the dust is, or the condition of the lander's parts. The images show brightness changes, not depth or damage.

images.title: InSight turning the colour of Mars

date.v: 23 October 2024 (part of a series that began 11 December 2018)

shows.v: InSight taking on the same reddish-brown colour as the rest of Mars. The dark halo its retrorockets scorched into the ground is fading, and dark stripes are tracks left by passing dust devils.

why.v: Monitoring dust at the surface shows how quickly a place changes over time.

learn.v: NASA explains that knowing how fast features fade helps scientists estimate how long craters have been there, and so how old a surface is.

cannot.v: Whether any of InSight's instruments could still work, or exactly how much dust lies on it.

instrument.v: Taken by the lander itself; the arm moves several times to build a full selfie. The camera is not named in NASA's description.

shows.v: The lander covered with far more dust than in its first selfie, taken in December 2018.

why.v: A final record before the team put the arm into its resting "retirement pose" because the dusty solar panels were producing less power.

learn.v: Comparing selfies over time shows how dust built up on the lander.

cannot.v: The exact power output, or the precise dust thickness, from the picture alone.
